depth.background: The **Women's Asia Cup** is the region's top continental cricket title, contested by India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and other Asian sides. India has traditionally been the dominant side but has faced tougher competition in recent editions as rivals like Sri Lanka and Bangladesh have improved. **Harmanpreet Kaur** has captained India Women through a period of rising expectations, including a maiden T20 World Cup near-miss, while **Smriti Mandhana** remains the team's most consistent batting star.
depth.why_it_matters: Squad announcements set the stage for how India will approach a tournament they're expected to win but haven't always dominated in recent years — continuity in leadership (Harmanpreet-Mandhana) signals the selectors are backing experience over a reset, even as depth gets tested through the India A pipeline.
depth.ripple_effects: Players named to the India A Rising Stars squad get a visible platform to push for full India selection; any strong showings there often shape squad changes for the following season's bigger tournaments, including future World Cups.
depth.why_now: The squad was announced within the last day, ahead of the tournament's build-up.
depth.watch_next: India's opening match schedule and squad fitness updates as the Asia Cup approaches.

key_terms.definition: The deputy leader of a cricket team, who takes over captaincy duties if the captain is unavailable and is often being groomed for the top job.

cards.title: Shafique and Babar Azam century stands haul Pakistan back into the 2nd Test after West Indies' 344
cards.what_happened: After Pakistan's bowlers dismissed West Indies for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) leading the recovery, with spinner **Sajid Khan** taking **4 for 85** — Pakistan's reply started shakily before Shafique and Babar Azam dug in. **Abdullah Shafique reached his sixth Test century (107 not out)**, while **Babar Azam batted to an unbeaten 86**, edging closer to what would be his first Test hundred in four years. Together they built an unbroken **168-run partnership** that carried Pakistan to **266 for 2** at the close of Day 2 — leaving them just **78 runs** behind West Indies' first-innings total with eight wickets still in hand, putting Pakistan firmly back in a series-deciding Test they needed to win.
key_points: West Indies were bowled out for **344** — Justin Greaves (73) and Roston Chase (70) top-scored.
Pakistan's **Sajid Khan** took 4/85 with spin to help wrap up the innings.
**Abdullah Shafique** made his **sixth Test century** (107 not out) opening the batting.
**Babar Azam** was unbeaten on **86**, closing in on his first Test century in four years.
Shafique and Babar's unbeaten **168-run stand** left Pakistan just **78 runs behind** at Day 2's close.
cards.moot: In Test cricket, a match can flip completely within a single session — being behind after Day 1 or Day 2 means far less than it looks like at the time.

thread.previously: We reported West Indies had recovered to 239/5 on Day 2 at Queen's Park Oval, with Justin Greaves anchoring the innings against dominant Pakistani spin bowling.
thread.changed: West Indies were eventually bowled out for 344 (Greaves 73, Roston Chase 70, Sajid Khan 4/85). In reply, Pakistan's openers turned the game around: Abdullah Shafique made a century and Babar Azam batted his way to 86 not out, an unbeaten 168-run stand that took Pakistan to 266/2 at Day 2's close — just 78 runs behind, with the series on the line.

depth.background: This is the **second and final Test** of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, played at Port of Spain's **Queen's Park Oval** — a series-decider after the first Test finished level. **Babar Azam**, Pakistan's long-time talisman and former captain, has endured a well-documented **four-year century drought** in Test cricket, making this innings a personal comeback story as much as a team one. **Abdullah Shafique** has quietly become Pakistan's most reliable opener over the same stretch.
depth.why_it_matters: With the series tied 1-1 after the first Test, this match decides the series outright — and Pakistan clawing back from a position of weakness, powered by Babar Azam's return to form, is exactly the kind of result that can define both a series and a struggling star's season.
depth.ripple_effects: A strong finish here would ease pressure on Babar Azam's place and form heading into Pakistan's next assignments, while a West Indies collapse in the field would raise fresh questions about their bowling depth outside the pace attack.
depth.why_now: Day 2 concluded on August 3 with this dramatic swing in momentum, setting up a pivotal Day 3.
depth.watch_next: Whether Babar Azam converts his overnight 86 into a full century on Day 3, and whether Pakistan can push for a first-innings lead.

key_terms.definition: In a Test match, the side that scores more runs in its first turn at bat gains a psychological and tactical edge for the rest of the game.

cards.title: Aiden Markram plays down talk he'll be named Lucknow Super Giants' next IPL captain
cards.what_happened: Asked directly about the vacant LSG captaincy on Monday, Aiden Markram said, **'I've got no idea,'** adding that the decision belongs to the franchise: **'They can decide whatever they think is best. There are some quality leaders in that group that we have there, so I'm not too fussed about it.'** He said 'the thoughts haven't been there just yet' on his own candidacy, despite being widely seen as a frontrunner given his experience captaining South Africa's T20 side. The vacancy opened after Rishabh Pant's trade to Delhi Capitals for Kuldeep Yadav left LSG without its previous leader. Mitchell Marsh, Australia's T20I captain and another senior figure in LSG's squad, is viewed as the other realistic contender for the role.
key_points: **Aiden Markram** downplayed speculation he'll take over as **Lucknow Super Giants (LSG)** captain for the next IPL season.
The captaincy question opened up after **Rishabh Pant** stepped down and was **traded to Delhi Capitals** for Kuldeep Yadav.
Markram said 'the thoughts haven't been there just yet' and pointed to **other 'quality leaders'** in the squad.
Australia's T20I captain **Mitchell Marsh**, also on LSG's roster, is seen as the other obvious contender.
Markram is South Africa's own **T20 captain**, making him a natural favorite despite his reluctance to commit.
cards.moot: In team sports, a leadership vacancy doesn't always get filled by the most obvious candidate — organizations often weigh squad dynamics and multiple qualified options rather than defaulting to reputation alone.

depth.background: Rishabh Pant had captained Lucknow Super Giants, but he was traded to Delhi Capitals in exchange for spinner Kuldeep Yadav, leaving the IPL franchise without a permanent leader heading into its next campaign. Markram, South Africa's white-ball captain, is widely regarded as a natural choice given his existing captaincy credentials, but LSG also has Australia's T20I captain Mitchell Marsh on its roster as an alternative option.
depth.why_it_matters: IPL captaincy decisions shape a franchise's on-field identity and tactical direction for years, and this appointment will be closely watched as one of the first major leadership calls of the post-Pant era at one of the league's higher-profile teams.
depth.ripple_effects: Whoever gets the armband affects LSG's leadership dynamic among a squad with multiple senior international captains, and the decision will likely factor into the league's ongoing pre-season trade and retention moves ahead of the next IPL auction cycle.
depth.why_now: The captaincy question has been open since Pant's trade earlier this year, and Markram's comments Monday are the first time he's addressed it directly in public.
depth.watch_next: Whether LSG announces a permanent captain before the next IPL season, and whether it's Markram, Marsh, or another squad member.

cards.title: Bangladesh's first Test tour of Australia in 23 years begins — without its fastest bowler
cards.what_happened: Bangladesh's Test squad departed for Australia on **August 1, 2026**, beginning what is the team's first Test tour of the country in **23 years**. The tour will not feature strike pacer **Nahid Rana**, who suffered a **Grade 2 side strain** during Bangladesh's second T20I against Zimbabwe on July 17 and has been ruled out of the entire two-match series. Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will also miss the opening Test, though he's expected to recover in time for the second. Uncapped quick **Musfik Hasan** has been named in the squad as cover. The tour schedule opens with a three-day warm-up match against a Cricket Australia XI at Darwin's DXC Arena from August 6-8, followed by the first Test in Darwin from August 13 and the second, and final, Test in Mackay from August 22.
key_points: Bangladesh departed for Australia on **August 1**, starting its **first Test tour of Australia in 23 years**.
Strike pacer **Nahid Rana** is ruled out of the **entire two-Test series** with a Grade 2 side strain suffered against Zimbabwe.
Wicketkeeper-batter **Liton Das** will miss the **first Test** but is expected to be fit for the second.
The tour opens with a **three-day warm-up match** in Darwin (Aug 6-8), before the **first Test in Darwin from August 13** and the second in **Mackay from August 22**.
Uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** has been added to the squad in Rana's absence.
cards.moot: A team's biggest test often arrives right when it's missing its most important player — depth in a squad matters as much as the star performers at the top of it.

depth.background: Bangladesh has toured Australia for Test cricket only rarely, and this trip marks the team's **first Test tour there in 23 years** — a landmark for a side still building credibility in the format's toughest conditions. Australian pitches, with their extra pace and bounce, are traditionally the hardest challenge for subcontinent teams, making a fit, in-form fast-bowling attack especially important. Nahid Rana, Bangladesh's quickest bowler, sustained his injury during the second T20I against Zimbabwe on **July 17**, and the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) confirmed on **July 25** that he would miss the tour entirely.
depth.why_it_matters: A historic first tour in over two decades is a meaningful test of how far Bangladesh's Test team has progressed, but losing its best fast bowler before a ball is bowled significantly weakens its chances against Australia's traditionally pace-heavy home conditions.
depth.ripple_effects: Bangladesh will likely lean more heavily on its remaining seam and swing bowlers, and results here could shape selection and confidence heading into the team's next assignments in the World Test Championship cycle.
depth.why_now: The squad's departure and tour schedule are unfolding this week, with the warm-up match starting within days.
depth.watch_next: How Bangladesh's depleted pace attack performs in the Darwin warm-up match ahead of the first Test on August 13.

cards.title: USA cricketer Akhilesh Reddy banned for eight years over Abu Dhabi T10 match-fixing
cards.what_happened: The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found **Akhilesh Reddy** guilty on **three counts** of the Anti-Corruption Code over his conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**. The tribunal ruled that he approached a teammate — referred to as 'Player A' — and asked him to **'give runs'**, meaning deliberately bowl in a way that concedes extra runs, allegedly at the behest of team management. When that player refused and instead reported the approach to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit, he was **dropped from the playing XI** shortly before the match in question. Reddy was also found to have **obstructed the investigation** by deleting relevant messages and call logs from his mobile phone once it began. His **eight-year ban is backdated to 21 November 2025**, the date of his provisional suspension, meaning he will not be eligible to return until **2033**.
key_points: USA international **Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy**, 26, has been banned from all cricket for **eight years**.
The ICC's Anti-Corruption Tribunal found him guilty over conduct during the **2025 Abu Dhabi T10 League**.
He asked a teammate to **'give runs'** — deliberately concede extra runs while bowling — allegedly on behalf of team management.
That teammate refused and instead **reported him to the ICC's Anti-Corruption Unit**, and was dropped from the XI as a result.
Reddy also **deleted messages and call logs** from his phone in an attempt to obstruct the investigation.
cards.moot: Corruption in cricket is usually stopped not by outsiders catching a fixer, but by a player on the inside refusing a corrupt approach and reporting it — which is why anti-corruption systems are built around protecting whistle-blowing teammates.

depth.background: The **Abu Dhabi T10** is a short, fast franchise tournament in the UAE that has repeatedly drawn scrutiny from cricket's anti-corruption authorities, because its **compressed matches, lower player profiles and heavy betting-market interest** make it an attractive target for fixers looking for less scrutiny than bigger leagues get. The **ICC Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU)** monitors global franchise leagues for approaches to players, officials and support staff, and has banned other players and even support-staff members from past T10 editions. Reddy, an Indian-origin American cricketer, was **provisionally suspended in November 2025** while the ICC investigated, and the case has now concluded with a tribunal verdict finding him guilty.
depth.why_it_matters: This is a case where the player who was approached to fix a match **refused and reported it**, showing cricket's anti-corruption reporting system working as intended instead of a cover-up only being uncovered later. It also reinforces that **smaller, lower-profile franchise leagues** like the Abu Dhabi T10 remain a soft target for match-fixing in global cricket.
depth.ripple_effects: The ban effectively ends Reddy's career with **USA Cricket**, a program trying to build credibility as it grows the sport domestically after co-hosting the 2024 T20 World Cup. It may push tournament organisers and the ICC toward tighter oversight of shorter, lower-salary franchise leagues where the temptation to fix is higher. The tribunal's findings also reference a **'team management'** instruction Reddy says he was acting on, which could mean further action against others is still to come.
depth.why_now: The tribunal's verdict and the eight-year sanction were announced today, closing out an investigation that began with Reddy's **provisional suspension back in November 2025**.

cards.title: Punjab Kings vice-captain Shashank Singh quits Chhattisgarh for Puducherry over 'disrespect'
cards.what_happened: Shashank Singh has left **Chhattisgarh** to represent **Puducherry** from the **2026-27 domestic season**, after the Chhattisgarh State Cricket Sangh (CSCS) issued him the NOC he needed to switch states. Singh told ESPNcricinfo the association gave him **no explanation** for excluding him from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad, and did not tell him why he was also missing from the **conditioning camp** for state probables. He said he had spent much of the past year managing a **shoulder injury and a fractured finger** and felt the board failed to support him through that recovery, adding that someone who won a **BCCI domestic award** deserves 'clarity, not ridicule'. Puducherry has agreed to let him play **white-ball cricket only** for now while he continues managing his fitness. The switch comes only months after Singh was made Punjab Kings' vice-captain in the IPL, raising his public profile just as his domestic-team relationship collapsed.
key_points: Shashank Singh, Punjab Kings' **vice-captain** and the **2023-24 BCCI best domestic white-ball all-rounder**, has left Chhattisgarh for **Puducherry**.
He was dropped from the **2026 Chhattisgarh Cricket Premier League** squad with **no explanation** given.
Singh says the state association gave him **no support** while he recovered from a shoulder injury and a fractured finger.
He will play **white-ball cricket only** this season while he keeps managing his fitness.

cards.moot: Even in a sport reshaped by IPL money, a player's week-to-week cricket future still runs through unglamorous state-association decisions — squad lists, fitness camps, medical support — and stardom doesn't exempt anyone from needing that relationship to actually work.

depth.background: Shashank Singh spent most of a long domestic career representing **Chhattisgarh**, a relatively young state cricket association carved out after the state's 2000 formation, before an explosive **2023 IPL season with Punjab Kings** turned him into a household name and, eventually, the franchise's **vice-captain**. He was named the **BCCI's best domestic white-ball all-rounder for 2023-24**, one of Indian domestic cricket's more prestigious individual honours. Players switch states in Indian domestic cricket occasionally and always need a **No-Objection Certificate (NOC)** from their current association, but a contracted IPL player of Singh's profile walking away is unusual and signals a real breakdown in the player-association relationship, not a routine transfer.
depth.why_it_matters: It is a rare, public breakdown between a **high-profile IPL player** and his home state association — the kind of selection dispute that usually stays behind closed doors in Indian domestic cricket. It highlights a real tension in the sport: state associations still control **Ranji Trophy and domestic league** selection, but IPL fame increasingly gives players enough leverage and options to simply leave if they feel mismanaged.
depth.ripple_effects: Chhattisgarh cricket loses one of its most recognisable modern players just as its own **Premier League** gets underway, raising uncomfortable questions about how the association manages injured or high-profile players. Puducherry, a smaller domestic side, instantly gains a proven IPL finisher for white-ball cricket. Other contracted IPL players watching a state board criticised in public may feel more confident seeking their own NOCs if they feel unsupported during injury layoffs.
depth.why_now: The move surfaces today because Indian domestic cricket's **2026-27 squad announcements** are being made this week, and Singh's exclusion from the Chhattisgarh Premier League squad was, in his telling, the final straw after months of being ignored by the association.
depth.watch_next: Watch whether the Chhattisgarh association responds publicly to Singh's comments, and whether he is named in a Puducherry white-ball squad in the coming weeks.

cards.title: BCCI will keep paying Ajinkya Rahane a ₹70,000 monthly pension even after his retirement
cards.what_happened: Days after Ajinkya Rahane announced his retirement from all international cricket, it's been confirmed he qualifies for the BCCI's **elite player pension scheme**, thanks to a long international career spanning **85 Tests, 90 ODIs, and 20 T20Is**. Under the board's **2022-revised pension structure**, he'll receive **₹70,000 per month** — up from the ₹50,000 top-tier former players received under the earlier scheme. There is one condition: if Rahane takes on a **full-time BCCI role**, such as a national or state coaching position or a selector's post, the monthly pension will be **temporarily suspended** for as long as he holds that job, and can resume once he leaves it.
key_points: Rahane qualifies for BCCI's **elite pension scheme** after playing **85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is** for India
He'll receive **₹70,000 a month** under the board's **2022-revised pension scheme**, up from ₹50,000 previously

cards.moot: Retirement benefits in sport aren't universal — they depend entirely on how wealthy and structured the specific league or board is, which is why the same career length can mean very different financial outcomes in different sports or countries.
